title: Climate Change, Mortality, and Adaptation: Evidence from Annual Fluctuations in Weather in the US
research_question: How do extreme daily temperatures affect annual mortality rates and residential energy consumption in the United States, and what are the implications of projected end-of-century climate change for human health and energy use, accounting for adaptive responses such as defensive expenditures on cooling?
data_description: The analysis combines four main data sources covering the continental United States. Mortality data come from the Compressed Mortality Files (1968-2002), comprising the universe of approximately 73.2 million death certificates with information by county of residence, age group, sex, race, cause, and year, along with population totals; these are supplemented by the 1972-1988 Multiple Cause of Death files. Residential energy consumption data are drawn from the U.S. Energy Information Administration's State Energy Data System, providing annual state-level energy consumption (in BTUs), prices, and expenditures from 1968-2002. Daily weather data (maximum and minimum temperature, precipitation) come from the NCDC Summary of the Day file, aggregated to 3,066 counties via inverse-distance weighting from stations within 200km of county centroids. Climate change predictions for 2070-2099 come from the Hadley Centre's CM3 model (A1FI scenario) and NCAR's CCSM3 model (A2 scenario). Units of observation are county-by-age-by-year for mortality and state-by-year for energy.
institutional_context: Climate change is projected to substantially alter the distribution of daily temperatures in the United States, with state-of-the-art models predicting roughly 40 additional days per year exceeding 90°F mean temperature by the end of the century under business-as-usual emissions scenarios. Human physiology responds to extreme heat and cold through thermoregulatory mechanisms, but temperatures outside normal ranges trigger excess mortality, particularly among infants and the elderly. Households can partially protect themselves against temperature extremes through self-protective expenditures, most notably residential energy consumption for air conditioning and heating. The penetration of cooling and heating technologies, the structure of housing, healthcare infrastructure, and population distribution across climate zones all shape how Americans experience temperature shocks. Integrated Assessment Models used in climate policy rely heavily on assumed parameters about these health and adaptation costs, motivating direct empirical estimates grounded in observed U.S. experience over 1968-2002 across all 48 continental states.
